newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-FISHING IN TROUBLED WATERS - Dil Vikas Finance Ltd.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-FISHING IN TROUBLED WATERS - Dil Vikas Finance Ltd.

text.p: FISHING IN TROUBLED WATERS - An analysis of the
economic factors driving stockmarket performance by R Balakrishnan, president of Dil Vikas Finance Ltd.
1997 clearly marks the beginning of the slowdown in the momentum of growth that the economy has witnessed since the inception of economic liberalisation.
The economy today is akin to a rubber band which is tightly stretched. Where it would give way is the key question.

As industrial growth is hampered by infrastructure bottlenecks and consumer spending is facing a slowdown on the back of rising retail prices, there is an air of uncertainty and hope as we approach the first full annual budget to be presented by the new "United Front" government.

The government has been busy trying to tell us that we are well on the growth path with a near 7 percent GDP which is sustainable over the next few years. However, the fine print of conditionalities surrounding this premise is questionable.
Taking all factors into consideration, it is clear that the current year is going to be one of the most difficult for industry in recent times.
Industry is showing very clear signs of cooling off, with the downtrend led by the consumer durables segment.
As rising prices of foodgrains and retail essentials eat into the pockets of the consumer (both rural and urban), there is a spin off on all other sectors.
Infrastructure, which on paper is thrown open for private sector, is struggling in one controversy or the other between different ideologies of various components of the "United Front" government.

The confidence (or rather, the lack of it) of the investors in the equities segment is beginning to tell on the corporate growth plans across the board. Banks, whilst awash in liquidity, are finding an easy avenue for investment in high yielding government paper which is virtually on tap.

With the government forcing the banks to lower PLR, the spread between the PLR and government paper is so thin that it is foolhardy to lend money to the corporate sector, with its attendant problems of new accounting norms and capital adequacy.

With the government's revenue target falling short on virtually every head (excise, income tax, dis-investment etc.,) and increasing expenditures (oil price hike causing dents in the oil pool account, increasing demands of state governments, higher crop subsidies etc.,), the fiscal deficit is being managed by the government borrowing more and more.
The spurt in bank liquidity (through incremental deposits and cuts in CRR) has been more than offset by government borrowings.

For the corporate sector as a whole, the most critical problem is that of money at reasonable cost. With the equity markets in a slumber since 1996 and likely to remain so for the near term, debt is the only alternative.
However, banks are willing to lend only at a range of 2 to 3 percent above the PLR, which industry finds unaffordable.

Further, with the government keeping its borrowing rates high (from 11 percent per annum in 1991, the five year paper is being issued at around 13.5 percent per annum), development banks raising money at close to 16 percent per annum, it is unlikely that we are going to see interest rates cooling off.

The only way it can happen is through large FDI flows, which are elusive thanks to dithering government will. Therefore, industry is coping with the slowdown by cutting production and drawing down inventories (often at huge discounts).
Unfortunately, exports are extremely sluggish, so this slowdown is going to tell on bottom lines. Imports of non-oil goods is decelerating, pointing to further signs of slow down.
Agriculture, after a negative growth (according to the third revision of the government statistics) is expected to show a modest growth this year.
A paradox is that after three years of boast of record reserve stocks of foodgrain (hopefully there was some wheat also in the stockpile) we have had to import wheat to arrest price rise in wheat.

Recent estimates of one of the government bodies put a grossly exaggerated weightage to the services sector. It is my reading that the services sector is badly affected in 1996/97, if one goes by the trends in the transportation sector. Thus, the overall growth for 1996/97 should be lower than in 1995/96.
Thus, our reading is that the economy would grow at a much lesser pace in 1997/98, with GDP growth being in the range of 5.5 to 6.0 percent.

The forthcoming budget has a lot at stake, in terms of policy statements. A clear mandate for active encouragement of private (domestic and foreign) participation in infrastructure is essential. Mere granting of fiscal concessions would be populist moves and are unlikely to be effective.

Multiplicity of controls and policy should be eliminated to provide a kickstart to this segment. If the recent controversy surrounding the Tata-Singapore Airlines venture is any indication of government policy, we are unlikely to make any headway.

There are bound to be a lot of sentiment-boosting announcements (which could include abatement of MAT, allowing buy back of shares, abolishment of double taxation of dividend, increasing protection to some industries through tariff changes, boosting of demand through lowering of excise on some industries, setting up of new bodies for boosting of capital markets, fiscal concessions etc.,) as the government is exhibiting an extraordinary concern for the state and the level of the stock markets.

The budget would attempt to boost capital market sentiment to create a favourable climb for whatever dis-investment possible as well as some large PSU issues through domestic and international floatations.

However, these would tend to be short-sighted measures caused by pressure from industry lobbies as well as the investment banking fraternity. I do not foresee any major announcement which can put back reforms on a sure footing.
Pressure to meet the impending supply of equity (from government as well as private sector) could even prompt diverting provident fund money into the highly immature and imperfect capital market.
Political instability is reflected in the centre's hesitancy to reduce subsidies and compounding the problems by resorting to hiked borrowings.

At the same time, the different state government's sacrifice revenues through populist policies (like imposing prohibition leading to loss of excise revenues, increasing the scope of free power to agriculture etc.,) compound the fiscal problem.

This government, which is so dependent on various factions, is compelled to cave into various demands, to retain power. Even statements like freeing the coal sector is followed by state governments announcing contradictory statements.

This multiplicity of controls on infrastructure is the biggest impediment to kicking off infrastructure growth as well as efficiency improvement in existing public sector undertakings. Exit policy for labour remains a distant dream.
Similarly, freeing up of insurance still remains a promise. In this kind of a political environment, it is hoping for too much to expect any definite positive steps.

In terms of corporate performance, an analysis of Dil Vikas Finance Ltd of the half yearly results (for the six months ended September 1996) of over 600 companies had indicated an overall negative earnings growth (in EPS terms) of around 5 percent (though the Aensex companies had reported a growth of 11 percent), with almost 40 percent of the companies not providing for MAT.
We expect the second half to be worse, with the earnings likely to exhibit a negative growth of around 8 to 10 percent.
From this level, there could be some improvement in 1997/98 should commodity prices look up. However, we do not have any reason to substantiate that things could be better in the coming fiscal year.

A study done by us indicates that the profitability of Indian companies is sliding downhill, as the other income component vanishes and rising interest burden takes its toll on a declining demand scenario.
The drastic fall in sanctions and disbursement by financial institutions, coupled with poor mobilisation of capital, indicates that industry is constrained in its growth.

Even if the capital market sentiments were to get better by the third quarter of calendar 1997, it can start having an impact only in 1998/99. Thus, 1997/98 is going to be characterised by tighter margins, dithering confidence in political stability and weakening economic outlook.
All in all, not a good mix.
It is highly possible that the stock markets could witness an immediate up-tick post budget.

However, if the speculator induced rally (aided by widely reported "package" from the Prime Minister, which turned out to be a "Jack-in-the-box" package) of the past two months is any indication, action is likely to be restricted to a narrow range of stocks, which because of their weightage in the indices, could give an illusion of momentum.
This illusion should evaporate as result information starts to come out by end April/early May which would lead to a significant downside correction.

Between now and the budget, the market is bound to be rumour driven, with "informed" advance news of things like share buy backs, granting of favourable status to "core" sectors, dilution of MAT, lowering of excise on select sectors etc.

This would provide useful opportunities to exit. Only the boldest, with a purely trading attitude may like to venture into the stock market between now and the budget. For the investor, the best policy would be, to "stay away".
However, there would be investors with "compulsions to invest". For them, we would recommend buying into cyclical stocks (paper, aluminium, petrochemicals) and await the up turn in the markets.
We would be neutral, for the present, on defensive investments like refineries and utilities. Demand for these are likely to taper off, as the slow down sets in.

Banking and Finance, though highly favoured at present, are not without risks. Poor corporate performance, coupled with liquidity problems across the board are likely to leave a dent on the asset quality of this sector.

The only positive which they could expect would be from not having to provide additional amounts for "mark to market". On cement and steel, we are negative at the moment, as increasing power and fuel costs, coupled with falling prices as a result of receding demand impairs their profitability.

However, the negative results in these sectors could provide some interesting valuation plays for the patient investor. The big hotel chains continue to do well, in the absence of any new room additions in the principal cities.
With demand likely to exceed the available supply of rooms, periodic price hikes would keep investors in this sector happy.

In most sectors, we expect better buying opportunities around May/June, rather than at this juncture. Debt still is attractive and is likely to out perform equities in the next twelve months or so. The key factor to watch for revival in equities is the breadth of the market.
Since 1995, all upside movements have been confined to the large pivotals. Volume data indicates that a handful of stocks account for more than 90 percent of the daily trading volumes.
Till such time as the breadth expands, the investors attention can only be focused on large capitalised liquid stocks. To buy small and mid-cap companies, one has to have a lot of patience and hopes.
A recent news item indicated that in January 1997, less than 2,000 stocks reported more than one trade during the month. This is surely not an encouraging sign.

All of these factors (technical and fundmental) do not point to allocating money to equities, yet. Any rally, which is induced by "favourable" announcements in the budget, should be used as an exit opportunity.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
